description: How markets connect — substitutes and complements, joint and competitive supply, and derived demand.
content_html:
Why Markets Are Linked

No market exists in isolation. When the price of petrol rises, demand for electric cars tends to increase. When the price of coffee falls, demand for coffee machines may rise. When farmers grow more wheat, the supply of straw — a by-product — also rises. These links between markets are called intermarket relationships, and understanding them is essential for predicting how prices and quantities adjust across the economy.

Substitute Goods

Substitute goods are goods that compete with each other. Butter and margarine are substitutes — if the price of butter rises sharply, consumers switch to margarine, so the demand for margarine increases. On a demand curve, this looks like a rightward shift in the demand for margarine: at every price, more margarine is now demanded. The equilibrium price of margarine rises and more is sold.

You can see this in the UK streaming market. When one major streaming service raises its monthly subscription price, consumers shop around and sign up for rival services instead. The demand curve for the rival shifts to the right — more subscribers at every price — pushing that rival’s equilibrium price up and its quantity of subscribers higher.

Key Fact

For substitute goods: if the price of Good A rises, demand for substitute Good B shifts RIGHT — raising the equilibrium price and quantity of B. The two markets move in the SAME direction for price.

Complementary Goods

Complementary goods are goods consumed jointly. Printers and printer ink are complements — you can’t use one without the other. If the price of printers falls dramatically, more printers are sold, and so demand for printer ink rises too. The demand curve for printer ink shifts to the right, raising the equilibrium price and quantity of ink.

Think about petrol and cars. If petrol prices rise sharply and stay high, the cost of running a car goes up. Consumers may delay buying new cars or switch to smaller, more fuel-efficient models. Demand for large petrol-engine cars shifts left — lower price and fewer sold. The two goods are complements, so their markets move in OPPOSITE directions: petrol up, car demand down.

Key Fact

For complementary goods: if the price of Good A rises, demand for complement Good B shifts LEFT — reducing the equilibrium price and quantity of B. The two markets move in OPPOSITE directions for quantity sold.

Students often confuse substitutes and complements. The test is simple: can you use one instead of the other (substitute), or do you need both together (complement)?

For substitutes, a price rise in one good INCREASES demand for the other — the demand curves move in the same direction. For complements, a price rise in one good DECREASES demand for the other — the demand curves move in opposite directions. In both cases, the mechanism is a shift in the demand curve, not a movement along it; the consumers’ preferences or the conditions of demand have changed.

Derived Demand

Derived demand occurs when the demand for one good comes from the demand for something else. Steel is demanded not because consumers enjoy steel for its own sake, but because firms need it to build cars, bridges and appliances. If the demand for new cars rises — say, because consumer confidence improves — car manufacturers need more steel and the demand for steel rises too. The demand curve for steel shifts to the right, raising steel prices and output.

Derived demand is also central to the labour market. A building company hires bricklayers not for their own sake but to build houses. If house prices rise and the property market booms, more houses are commissioned, demand for bricklayers rises, and wages in the construction sector are pushed up. The demand for labour is always a derived demand — it flows from the demand for the final product or service.

Composite Demand

Composite demand arises when a good is demanded for more than one purpose. Milk is a classic example: it is demanded for drinking, for making cheese, for making butter and for producing yoghurt. If demand for cheese rises sharply — perhaps because a health trend promotes high-protein diets — more milk is diverted to cheese production. Less milk is available for other uses, so the price of drinking milk and butter rises too. A single resource being pulled in different directions creates competition between those uses.

Land illustrates composite demand clearly. Farmland is demanded for growing crops, for building houses and for renewable energy projects such as solar farms. When house-building programmes expand, more land is bid away from agriculture. This reduces the supply of land for farming, pushing up the cost of growing food and ultimately raising food prices.

Joint supply (also called joint production) occurs when producing one good necessarily produces another as a by-product. Beef and leather are the classic example: both come from cattle. If the demand for beef rises, farmers rear more cattle, and the supply of leather increases automatically. On a supply-and-demand diagram, the supply of leather shifts to the right, reducing the equilibrium price of leather and increasing the quantity sold.

The North Sea oil industry provides a further example: crude oil extraction yields natural gas as a by-product. When oil production increases, the supply of natural gas rises too, even if the demand for gas has not changed. This can depress gas prices and affect the profitability of gas producers.

Competitive supply occurs when two goods compete for the same limited resources. A farmer with a fixed area of land must choose between growing wheat or oilseed rape. If the price of wheat rises, it becomes more profitable to grow wheat. The farmer switches land from oilseed rape to wheat, so the supply of oilseed rape falls — its supply curve shifts left and its price rises. The two markets move in opposite directions for quantity supplied.

How a Change in One Market Ripples Through Others

Real-world economic events rarely stay confined to a single market. Consider what happened when global semiconductor shortages emerged after 2020. Semiconductors are in composite demand — they are used in cars, laptops, fridges, smartphones and medical equipment. When supply fell sharply, prices rose across all these markets. Car manufacturers were forced to pause production lines because they could not obtain the chips they needed (derived demand at work: fewer chips → fewer cars). Meanwhile, rival producers of less chip-intensive goods gained a competitive edge as consumers switched to alternatives (substitute goods at work).

Tracing these chains is exactly what examiners want to see: identify the initial change, state how it affects the demand or supply curve in the first market, then follow the ripple into linked markets, naming the relationship type (substitute, complement, joint supply, competitive supply or derived demand) at each step.
exam_tip_html: When an “Analyse” or “Evaluate” question asks how a change in one market affects another, use a clear chain of reasoning: state the initial change, identify the type of relationship (substitute, complement, joint supply, competitive supply, derived demand), then say which curve shifts in the second market and in which direction, before stating the new equilibrium outcome for price and quantity. A common error is to describe the relationship correctly but then fail to follow it through to the equilibrium — always end with “therefore the equilibrium price rises/falls and the quantity sold increases/decreases.” For a 9- or 12-mark evaluate question, acknowledge that the size of the price change in the first market determines how large the ripple effect will be in the second, and consider whether the goods are close or distant substitutes or complements.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Substitute goods compete to satisfy the same want: a price rise in one shifts demand for the substitute to the right, raising its equilibrium price and quantity. Complementary goods are used together: a price rise in one shifts demand for the complement to the left, lowering its equilibrium price and quantity.
  • Derived demand and composite demand are demand-side concepts in connected markets: derived demand links the demand for inputs to the demand for final goods; composite demand means a single resource pulled into competing uses, so higher demand in one use reduces availability and raises price in others.
  • Joint supply and competitive supply show how producers’ decisions link markets: joint supply means more of one good automatically means more of the by-product; competitive supply means more of one good means less of the rival, because both compete for the same resources.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of two substitute goods?
A) Bread and butter
B) Cars and petrol
C) Tea and coffee
D) Printers and printer ink
practice_questions.marks: C) Tea and coffee [1 mark]. Tea and coffee can be consumed in place of each other to satisfy the same want (a hot drink). Bread and butter, cars and petrol, and printers and printer ink are all examples of complementary goods.

practice_questions.text: The price of beef rises from £5 per kg to £6 per kg, and the quantity of beef demanded falls from 200 kg to 160 kg. Calculate the percentage change in the quantity of beef demanded.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for correct method: percentage change = (change in quantity ÷ original quantity) × 100 = (−40 ÷ 200) × 100.
1 mark for the correct answer of −20% (a fall of 20%).

practice_questions.text: Explain why an increase in the demand for new houses is likely to lead to an increase in the demand for bricklayers.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying derived demand: the demand for bricklayers is derived from the demand for houses.
1 mark for development: when demand for houses rises, builders need to hire more bricklayers to complete additional construction projects.
1 mark for further development or consequence: this shifts the demand curve for bricklayers to the right, putting upward pressure on bricklayers' wages and increasing the number of bricklayers employed.

practice_questions.text: A UK firm produces both rapeseed oil and rapeseed meal using the same crop. Explain how a rise in the global price of rapeseed oil is likely to affect the market for rapeseed meal.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying joint supply: rapeseed oil and rapeseed meal are produced jointly from the same crop.
1 mark for chain of reasoning: a rise in the global price of rapeseed oil increases the profitability of producing rapeseed, so farmers plant more.
1 mark for supply shift: as more rapeseed is crushed, the supply of rapeseed meal (the by-product) increases, shifting its supply curve to the right.
1 mark for equilibrium outcome: the equilibrium price of rapeseed meal falls and the quantity sold rises.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a significant rise in the price of petrol is likely to affect the markets for electric cars and car insurance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Develops two clear chains of reasoning with correct identification of relationship types (substitute for electric cars; complement for car insurance via car ownership). Accurately traces the demand or supply shift in each linked market through to the new equilibrium price and quantity. May note that the size of the effect depends on how close a substitute electric cars are for petrol cars, and whether the price rise is seen as permanent.
Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies at least one relationship type correctly and follows it through to an equilibrium outcome. The second market may be less fully developed or the chain of reasoning may contain a minor gap.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies that petrol and electric cars are substitutes and that demand for electric cars rises, but does not reach a conclusion about equilibrium or does not address the car insurance market.
Emerging (1 mark): Makes a simple relevant point (e.g. “if petrol is more expensive, people may buy electric cars”) without developing a chain of reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
'A rise in the price of one good will always benefit the producers of a related good.' Evaluate this statement with reference to the different types of intermarket relationships.
In your answer, consider arguments for and against the statement and reach a supported judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Substitute goods: if Good A's price rises, consumers switch to substitute Good B, shifting B's demand curve right. Producers of B benefit from a higher equilibrium price and greater sales revenue.
• Joint supply by-product: if higher prices for Good A lead to greater production, the by-product B is also produced in greater quantities. If demand for B is inelastic, the price fall is small and producers of B still earn reasonable revenue.

Arguments against:
• Complementary goods: if Good A's price rises, demand for complement Good B falls (demand curve shifts left). Producers of B face lower prices and sell fewer units — they are harmed, not helped.
• Competitive supply: if Good A's price rises and farmers/producers switch resources to A, less of Good B is produced. Whilst B's price may rise (supply shifts left because fewer resources are devoted to it — the mechanism is higher opportunity cost of production, not higher input costs), overall profitability depends on the price elasticity of B.
• Derived demand: if Good A is an input derived from the demand for a final good, and the final good's price rise is due to falling demand (not rising supply), then demand for the input falls — producers of A are harmed.

Judgement:
The statement is too broad to be always true. It depends on the type of relationship: substitute producers benefit, complement producers lose out. It also depends on the SIZE of the price change (a small rise may trigger little switching) and whether the goods are CLOSE or DISTANT substitutes/complements (close substitutes experience larger demand shifts). A supported conclusion should weigh at least two relationship types against each other.

Mastering (8–9 marks): Analyses at least three relationship types with accurate supply-and-demand reasoning, reaches a well-supported judgement that references the conditions under which the statement holds.
Secure (5–7 marks): Analyses two relationship types with broadly accurate reasoning, attempts a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies two relationship types but the reasoning may lack rigour; limited or unsupported judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Simple relevant points about one relationship type; no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of goods are consumed together, so that a rise in the price of one reduces demand for the other?
Beef and leather both come from cattle. When the demand for beef rises, the supply of leather automatically increases. What type of supply relationship is this?
Demand for bricklayers rises because demand for new houses has increased. This is an example of _____ demand.
When two goods compete for the same productive resources, producing more of one reduces the supply of the other. This is called _____ supply.
Match each intermarket relationship to its definition:
right: Goods that can replace each other, so a price rise in one raises demand for the other
Goods used together, so a price rise in one lowers demand for the other
Demand for a good used for several different purposes, creating competing uses for the same resource

flashcard_questions.a: Goods that can replace each other; a price rise in one increases demand for the other.
Goods consumed together; a price rise in one reduces demand for the other.

flashcard_questions.q: If the price of tea rises, what happens to demand for coffee (a substitute)?
flashcard_questions.a: Demand for coffee shifts right — higher equilibrium price and more coffee sold.

flashcard_questions.q: If the price of printers falls, what happens to demand for printer ink (a complement)?
flashcard_questions.a: Demand for printer ink shifts right — higher equilibrium price and more ink sold.
Demand for a good that arises because it is needed to produce another good or service.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the demand for steel described as derived demand?
flashcard_questions.a: It is demanded to make cars and appliances, not for its own sake.
Demand for a good used for several purposes, so competing uses bid against each other.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a good in composite demand and explain why it qualifies.
flashcard_questions.a: Milk — it is demanded for several competing purposes (drinking, cheese, butter, yoghurt), so rising demand in one use reduces availability for others.
When producing one good automatically produces another as a by-product.

flashcard_questions.q: Beef and leather are produced jointly. If demand for beef rises, what happens to the supply of leather?
flashcard_questions.a: Supply of leather shifts right — more leather produced as a by-product.
When two goods compete for the same resources, so more of one means less of the other.

flashcard_questions.q: A farmer switches land from oilseed rape to wheat when wheat prices rise. What happens to the supply of oilseed rape?
flashcard_questions.a: Supply of oilseed rape shifts left — less produced, price rises.

flashcard_questions.q: For substitutes: if Price A rises, which way does the demand curve for Good B shift?
flashcard_questions.a: Right — more of Good B is demanded at every price.

flashcard_questions.q: For complements: if Price A rises, which way does the demand curve for Good B shift?
flashcard_questions.a: Left — less of Good B is demanded at every price.

glossary_terms.definition: The relationships between different markets, where a change in price, demand or supply in one market affects conditions in another.
Goods that can be used in place of each other to satisfy the same want, so that a rise in the price of one increases demand for the other.
Goods that are used together, so that a rise in the price of one reduces demand for the other.
Demand for a good or factor of production that arises not for its own sake but because it is needed to produce another good or service.
Demand for a good that can be used for several different purposes, so that a rise in demand for one use reduces the supply available for other uses.
A situation where the production of one good automatically results in the production of another good at the same time.
A situation where two goods compete for the same productive resources, so that producing more of one reduces the supply of the other.
